summary: This note describes the Heian period of Japanese history, beginning in 794 when Emperor Kanmu moved the capital to Heian-kyō (present-day Kyōto). It covers the decline of Chinese institutional influence after 838, the rise of Fujiwara dominance over the imperial court, and the growing power of provincial warrior families and shōen estates. The note frames the period as a high point of Japanese culture and the precursor to samurai rule.
one_line: Overview of Japan's Heian period (794 onward), covering the move to Heian-kyō, Fujiwara dominance, the end of Tang missions, and the rise of the warrior class.
key_facts: The Heian period began in 794 A.D. after the capital of Japan was moved to Heian-kyō (present-day Kyōto) by Emperor Kanmu, the 50th emperor.
Kanmu first tried to move the capital to Nagaoka-kyō, but a series of disasters befell the city, prompting a second relocation to Heian.
In 838 the imperial-sanctioned missions to Tang China, which had begun in 630, ended, marking the effective end of Chinese influence.
The Soga clan had taken control of the throne in the sixth century, and the Fujiwara had intermarried with the imperial family by the ninth century.
During the reign of Emperor Daigo (897-930), the Fujiwara regency was suspended as he ruled directly.
Nominally sovereignty lay in the emperor, but in fact power was wielded by the Fujiwara nobility.
As early as 939 A.D., Taira no Masakado led an uprising in the eastern province of Hitachi that threatened the central government.
Almost simultaneously in 939, Fujiwara no Sumitomo rebelled in the west.
Kyōto remained the imperial capital for the next 1,000 years after Kammu moved the capital there.
Nara was abandoned after only 70 years, in part due to the ascendancy of Dōkyō and the encroaching secular power of Buddhist institutions there.
The early Heian period (784–967) continued Nara culture, and the Heian capital was patterned on the Chinese Tang capital at Chang'an but on a larger scale.
The ritsuryō system attempted to recreate the Tang imperium in Japan, despite the "tremendous differences in the levels of development between the two countries".
Following Kammu's death in 806, two new offices were established: the Emperor's Private Office and the Metropolitan Police Board, which replaced the largely ceremonial imperial guard units.
By the early Heian period, shōen had obtained legal status, and large religious establishments sought clear titles in perpetuity, waiver of taxes, and immunity from government inspection.
